title.en: Possession (का / के / की, अपना) and 'to have' (के पास)

summary.en: Possessive का/के/की agrees forward with the thing owned, अपना refers back to the clause's subject, and के पास expresses 'to have' without a 'have' verb.

body.en:
From *आँगन हवेली*, season 1.

**1. *का / के / की* agrees forward with the thing possessed (never the owner!):**
Think of *का* (`kā`, 'of / -'s') as an `-आ` adjective glued after the owner. Its ending looks **forward** at the noun that follows:
- Masculine singular direct: *काग़ज़ का रजिस्टर* (`kāgaz kā rajisṭar`, 'paper register'), *आँगन का दरवाज़ा* ('courtyard door').
- Feminine (singular or plural!): *गेट की घंटी* (`geṭ kī ghanṭī`, 'the gate bell'), *पीतल की आठ चाबियाँ* ('eight brass keys').
- Masculine plural or before another postposition: *तीन गेस्टहाउसों के चित्र* ('drawings of three guesthouses'), *आँगन के पौधों का ख़्याल* ('care of the courtyard plants').
Pronouns fuse this ending directly: *मेरा / मेरे / मेरी* ('my'), *तुम्हारा* ('your'), *आपका* ('your [polite]'), *हमारा* ('our'). Whenever the owner is also the **subject** of the sentence, Hindi swaps all of those for reflexive *अपना / अपने / अपनी* ('one's own'): *वह आदमी अपना सूटकेस वापस लिए बिना क्यों भाग गया?* ('why did that man run off without taking **his own** suitcase back?').

**2. How Hindi says 'to have' (no verb 'have'!):**
- For **portable objects, keys, money, or spare items**, use `[owner in oblique] + के पास ... है/हैं` (literally 'near X, Y is'): *मेरे पास बस यही कोट है* ('I only have this coat'), *मेरे पास दो नरम तकिये हैं* ('I have two soft pillows').
- For **needs and wants**, use `[person] + को ... चाहिए`: *मुझे बस यही चाहिए था* ('that is just what I needed').
